• Learning simple greetings.

lines.zh: 請問你是陳月美小姐嗎？
lines.py: Qǐngwèn nǐ shì Chén Yuèměi xiǎojiě ma?
Shìde. Xièxie nǐ lái jiē wǒmen.
Nǐ hǎo. Wǒ xìng Wáng, jiào Kāiwén.

lines.zh: 你們好。歡迎你們來臺灣。
lines.py: Nǐmen hǎo. Huānyíng nǐmen lái Táiwān.

translation.en: Excuse me, are you Miss Chen Yuemei?
Yes. Thank you for coming to pick us up.
You're welcome. My name is Minghua Li.
Hi, my surname is Wang. My first name is Kaiwen.
How are you? Welcome to Taiwan.

lines.zh: 謝謝。很好喝。請問這是什麼茶？

This is Oolong tea. Taiwanese like to drink tea. Kaiwen, how about you Japanese people?
I am sorry. Which country are you from?
Kaiwen, would you like to drink coffee?
Thank you. I don't drink coffee. I like to drink tea.

blocks.en: I. Ways to Ask Questions in Chinese — A. Asking Questions with A-not-A

paras.text: Function: The A-not-A form of making a question is the most neutral way to ask a question in Chinese and closest to yes/no questions in English.

items.py: Wáng Xiānshēng yào bú yào hē kāfēi?
items.en: Does Mr. Wang want to have some coffee?

items.py: Zhè shì bú shì Wūlóng chá?

items.zh: 臺灣人喜歡不喜歡喝茶？
items.py: Táiwān rén xǐhuān bù xǐhuān hē chá?
items.en: Do Taiwanese people like to drink tea?

paras.text: Structures: The “A” in the structure refers to the first verbal element.

rows.en: Does he want to drink coffee?

rows.py: Nǐ shì bú shì Rìběn rén?

paras.text: Usage: When the verbal element in an A-not-A question is disyllabic (XY), the second syllable (Y) can be dropped in the first “A” of the pattern, so “XY-not-XY” is the same as “X-not-XY”. For example, 你喜歡不喜歡我？ Nǐ xǐhuān bù xǐhuān wǒ? is the same as 你喜不喜歡我？ Nǐ xǐ bù xǐhuān wǒ? (Do you like me?)

blocks.en: B. Asking Questions with 嗎 ma

paras.text: Function: Questions can be formed using the question particle 嗎 ma. It is usually used for short questions.

items.en: Are you here to pick us up?

paras.text: Structures: SENTENCE + 嗎 ma? The sentence in 嗎 ma questions can be either in the affirmative or negative.

items.py: Nǐ bú shì Táiwān rén ma?

paras.text: Usage: The A-not-A question form indicates no assumption, and is used for neutral inquiries or longer inquiries. It does not take a 嗎 ma question particle at the end of the sentence. One cannot say *這是不是茶嗎？ Zhè shì bú shì chá ma? (‘Is this tea?’). 嗎 ma questions, by contrast, are used for short inquiries. But in most cases, these two forms of question are often interchangeable.

items.en: Do you want to drink tea?

items.py: Nǐmen yào bú yào hē Wūlóng chá?
items.en: Do you want to drink Oolong tea?

blocks.title: 練習 Exercise
blocks.instruction: Complete questions using 嗎 ma based on the responses to the right. (Question ＿＿＿？ → Response)

blocks.en: II. Answering Questions in Chinese — A. Affirmative Answers

paras.text: Affirmative answers can be formed by repeating the main verb in the question, followed by a sentence in the affirmative, e.g.,

a.zh: 他是不是臺灣人？／他是臺灣人嗎？
a.py: Tā shì bú shì Táiwān rén? / Tā shì Táiwān rén ma?

a.zh: 你喜不喜歡臺灣？／你喜歡臺灣嗎？
a.py: Nǐ xǐ bù xǐhuān Táiwān? / Nǐ xǐhuān Táiwān ma?

a.zh: 王先生是不是日本人？／王先生是日本人嗎？
a.py: Wáng Xiānshēng shì bú shì Rìběn rén? / Wáng Xiānshēng shì Rìběn rén ma?

b.py: Shì, Wáng Xiānshēng shì Rìběn rén.

a.zh: 他喝不喝烏龍茶？／他喝烏龍茶嗎？
a.py: Tā hē bù hē Wūlóng chá? / Tā hē Wūlóng chá ma?

paras.text: In Chinese, short answers in the affirmative can be made by simply repeating the verb from the question.

a.py: Tā xǐhuān bù xǐhuān hē chá?

items.prompt: 臺灣人喜歡不喜歡喝茶？

blocks.en: B. Negative Replies with 不 bù

paras.text: Negative replies can be formed by repeating the main verb in its negative form, i.e., 不 bù + verb, followed by a sentence in the negative. 不 bù is an adverb which is placed before a verb or another adverb, e.g.,

a.py: Tā shì bú shì Lǐ Xiānshēng?

b.py: Bú shì, tā bú shì Lǐ Xiānshēng.
b.en: No, he is not Mr. Li.

a.py: Lǐ Xiǎojiě shì bú shì Táiwān rén?

b.zh: 不是，李小姐不是臺灣人。
b.py: Bú shì, Lǐ Xiǎojiě bú shì Táiwān rén.
b.en: No, Miss Li is not Taiwanese.

paras.text: In Chinese, the answer to a question can consist of just the verb in the question asked.

a.py: Tā yào bú yào hē kāfēi?
a.en: Does he want to drink coffee?

a.zh: 你喜歡不喜歡喝烏龍茶？
a.py: Nǐ xǐhuān bù xǐhuān hē Wūlóng chá?
a.en: Do you like to drink Oolong tea?

a.py: Chén Xiǎojiě shì bú shì Měiguó rén?

paras.text: Usage: There are some exceptions to the rules above. For example, when the verb is 姓 xìng “to be surnamed” or 叫 jiào “to be called”. When the question is 他姓李嗎？ Tā xìng Lǐ ma? ‘Is he surnamed Li?’, the negative reply should be 不姓李 Bú xìng Lǐ ‘(He is) not surnamed Li.’, rather than *不姓 bú xìng. When the question is 李先生叫開文嗎？ Lǐ Xiānshēng jiào Kāiwén ma? ‘Is Mr. Li called Kaiwen?’, the negative reply should be 不叫開文 Bú jiào Kāiwén ‘(He is) not called Kaiwen.’, rather than *不叫 bú jiào.

paras.text: Function: The adverb 很 hěn modifies state verbs (Vs).

items.zh: 臺灣人很喜歡喝烏龍茶。
items.py: Táiwān rén hěn xǐhuān hē Wūlóng chá.
items.en: Taiwanese people like to drink Oolong tea.

paras.text: Structures: The adverb 很 hěn is placed before state verbs (Vs) as follows: Subject 很 hěn + State Verb.

Usage: In general, adjectival state verbs must be preceded by either 不 or intensifiers. When no particular intensity is intended, they are preceded by 很 hěn. That is, 很 hěn + stative verb means ‘very stative verb’ (very expensive, very good, very tall, etc.) and sometimes it just means a stative verb. When 很 is intended to actually mean ‘very’, it is typically stressed in speech.

items.hint: 陳小姐很喜歡喝茶。 — Yes, she does.
他很喜歡臺灣。 — Yes, he does.
他很喜歡。 — Yes, he (actually) does.

blocks.en: IV. Contrastive Questions with 呢 ne

paras.text: Function: The 呢 ne question is a tag question with a short form following a statement.

items.py: Wǒ yào hē chá, nǐ ne?
items.en: I want to drink tea, and you?

items.py: Tā bù hē kāfēi, Chén Xiǎojiě ne?
items.en: He does not drink coffee. What about Miss Chen?

items.zh: 王先生是日本人，李先生呢？
items.py: Wáng Xiānshēng shì Rìběn rén, Lǐ Xiānshēng ne?
items.en: Mr. Wang is Japanese. What about Mr. Li?

paras.text: Structures: 1. Same predicate, different subjects — S1 V O, S2 呢 ne?

items.py: Tā shì Měiguó rén, nǐ ne?

items.en: He likes us. How about you?

paras.text: 2. Same subject, different predicates — S V O1, O2 呢 ne?

items.py: Nǐ xǐhuān hē chá, kāfēi ne?
items.en: You like to drink tea. How about coffee?

items.py: Tā bù hē kāfēi, chá ne?
items.en: He doesn't drink coffee. How about tea?

Task: Pair up with a classmate, say hello, and introduce yourself. Then ask him/her for his/her name, where s/he is from, and introduce him/her to the class.
Goal: Learning to ask whether someone likes to drink tea or coffee.

Task: Use the A-not-A form 喜歡不喜歡 to ask a classmate whether s/he likes to drink tea/coffee. If the answer is in the affirmative, then treat him/her to one. If the answer is in the negative, give other options.

blocks.en: Bits of Chinese Culture — Tea Culture

paras.text: “Come over for some tea!” is a common phrase used much like the phrase in English, “You really have to drop by my place sometime for a cup of coffee”. In Taiwan, friends gather around a table with a tea set on it in their free time and drink tea. They drink the tea from delicate, little teacups and might discuss its fragrance and taste. Chatting over tea is a favorite way of the Chinese to bond and keep abreast of the latest things in their lives.

At home, many people make themselves a cup of hot tea or prepare a pot for the family for after-dinner conversation. Many people like to start off the day at the office with a cup of tea. Those with a more discerning palate might make tea using tea leaves, while teabags probably suffices for others. In the end, they all enjoy a nice cup of hot tea.
In the shade of old trees in parks or near temples, you can find folks sitting around small tables drinking tea and snacking on melon seeds. Tea is an everyday part of life of the people of Taiwan.

paras.text: It is customary for Chinese to call friends and loved ones by nicknames. The character “老” lǎo is sometimes added before the last name or “小” xiǎo placed in front of the second character of the given name to form nicknames. Due to the influence of the Taiwanese dialect, nicknames in Taiwan are often formed by placing the character “阿” ā in front of the name or the second character of the given name is repeated. For example, someone by the name of “陳文華” could be nicknamed “老陳,” “小陳,” “小華,” “華華,” or “阿華.”

blocks.en: 2. Third Tone Change 三聲變調

paras.text: (1) When two characters with third tones are found together, the first third tone is pronounced with a second tone as in these two examples in this lesson: 小姐 xiǎojiě (ˇ + ˇ → ˊ ˇ)　你好 nǐ hǎo (ˇ + ˇ → ˊ ˇ)
Despite the change in pronunciation, however, it is still marked as a third tone in pinyin.
(2) Rules for third-tone changes 三聲變調原則 (the tone in parentheses is the tone actually pronounced):

The tone for 不 bù changes depending on the tone of the character that follows it. When 不 bù is followed by a character with a first, second, or third tone, 不 bù is pronounced and the pinyin marked with a fourth tone (ˋ). When 不 bù is followed by a character with a fourth tone, it is pronounced and the pinyin marked with a second tone (ˊ).

head: 不 bù + 1st, 2nd or 3rd tone → 不 pronounced with 4th tone (4th tone mark)
不 bù + 4th tone → 不 pronounced with 2nd tone (2nd tone mark)
rows: 不喝咖啡 bù hē kāfēi
不喜歡 bù xǐhuān · (對)不起 (duì)bùqǐ

blocks.en: Introduction to Chinese Characters — Basic Chinese Strokes

paras.text: Chinese calligraphy consists of eight basic strokes. These are also the basic strokes of Chinese characters. These eight basic strokes are “horizontal” (橫 héng), “vertical” (豎 shù), “brush left” (撇 piě), “press down and drag” (捺 nà), “dot” (點 diǎn), “flick” (挑 tiǎo), “hook” (鉤 gōu), and “corner fold” (折 zhé). They are used to teach beginners to write Chinese characters.
